reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours: Breast Tumours
clinicalPearls: A benign, well-circumscribed overgrowth of disorganised but otherwise normal breast tissue, comprising glandular, fibrous and adipose elements.
Often presents as a soft, mobile, painless mass or as an incidental screening finding, most commonly in women in their fourth to fifth decade.
The mammographic appearance is characteristic: an encapsulated lesion containing both fat and soft-tissue density, described as a 'breast within a breast'.
A thin radiolucent capsule separating the lesion from surrounding tissue supports the diagnosis.
Because it contains all normal breast constituents, core biopsy can appear deceptively 'normal', making radiological correlation essential.
Proportions of fat, fibrous stroma and glandular tissue vary, giving rise to the synonyms fibroadenolipoma and adenolipoma.
Treatment is reassurance for typical asymptomatic lesions, with excision reserved for large, symptomatic or diagnostically uncertain masses.
Multiple hamartomas, particularly with mucocutaneous features, should prompt consideration of Cowden syndrome.
reference.pathophysiology: A breast hamartoma is a developmental, tumour-like malformation rather than a true neoplasm, arising from the localised disorganised proliferation of the mature tissue elements normally present in the breast. Ducts, lobules, fibrous stroma and mature adipose tissue are haphazardly arranged within a thin pseudocapsule that demarcates the lesion from adjacent parenchyma. Because the constituent tissues are cytologically normal, the hamartoma behaves as a slowly enlarging, well-defined mass. Its recognition rests largely on the interplay of fatty and glandular densities on imaging, since histology of a small sample may be indistinguishable from ordinary breast tissue.
additionalInvestigations: Mammography to demonstrate the mixed-density encapsulated lesion
Breast ultrasound to assess the heterogeneous circumscribed mass
Core needle biopsy with radiological-pathological correlation
Breast MRI for large or atypical lesions
Excisional biopsy when the diagnosis is uncertain
Assessment for features of Cowden syndrome if multiple lesions
redFlags: Rapid or asymmetric enlargement of a previously stable mass
Suspicious microcalcification or an intralesional solid nodule
Skin tethering, nipple retraction or fixity
Discordance between benign biopsy and suspicious imaging
Multiple hamartomas with mucocutaneous stigmata of Cowden syndrome
reference.prognosis: Breast hamartoma is benign with an excellent prognosis, and simple excision is curative when required. Malignancy arising within a hamartoma is rare and generally reflects an incidental coexisting lesion rather than transformation of the hamartoma itself.
pitfalls: Interpreting deceptively 'normal' core biopsy tissue as a benign result without imaging correlation
Mistaking a hamartoma for a simple fibroadenoma or lipoma
Overlooking an incidental carcinoma developing within the lesion
Failing to recognise the 'breast within a breast' mammographic sign
Missing the link between multiple hamartomas and Cowden syndrome
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Breast Tumours (current edition)
Standard textbook of breast imaging on circumscribed masses
National guidance on assessment of benign breast lesions
management: Confirm the diagnosis on mammography showing the characteristic encapsulated mixed fat and soft-tissue 'breast within a breast' appearance, with radiological-pathological correlation because core biopsy may appear deceptively normal
Reassure and observe asymptomatic, radiologically typical lesions
Offer surgical excision for large, symptomatic, enlarging, or diagnostically uncertain masses, which is curative
Arrange interval imaging surveillance for conservatively managed lesions
Assess for Cowden syndrome and consider genetic referral when hamartomas are multiple or syndromic features are present
